decision: Which approach best resolves: Choose the write-concurrency strategy for SQLite in a Digital Sales Room where a Python backend serves the UI and must log every write to an audit table.

state.problem: Choose the write-concurrency strategy for SQLite in a Digital Sales Room where a Python backend serves the UI and must log every write to an audit table.

candidate_solutions.single_writer_wal: One long-lived backend process is the ONLY writer to the shared SQLite file, in WAL mode with a generous busy_timeout. Sub-agents never write the shared database: they write source code and pytest tests that run against a throwaway temp database per test. The audit log is written by the backend in the same transaction as the data change, so audit rows can never be lost or reordered relative to the change they describe.
candidate_solutions.shared_db_direct_writes: Sub-agents and tests may write the shared SQLite file directly, in WAL mode with busy_timeout and retry-on-busy. Maximally convenient for ad-hoc inspection, but audit rows can be written by a process other than the one that changed the data, and an abandoned test can leave the shared file locked or dirty.
candidate_solutions.per_writer_databases: Each git worktree gets its own SQLite file and audit logs are merged afterwards. Zero cross-process contention, but merging is lossy on ordering, audit ids can collide across worktrees, and the running UI cannot show a coherent audit trail.

context.conclusion_already_established: Sub-agents write CODE, not rows in the shared database. Their tests use per-test temporary databases. Therefore the only production writer is the backend process, and the real concurrency question is just multiple backend workers plus test runs.

decision: Which approach best resolves: Porting 12 already-built feature branches onto the new plugin host. Survey of what each needed from the old shared api.py: 9 of 12 registered a FastAPI exception handler via @app.exception_handler for their own domain error type (RuleError, LibraryError, AccessError, CrmError, SearchError, PermissionDenied, ...). FastAPI exception handlers can only be attached to the app object, not to an APIRouter, so a feature cannot attach its own error mapping without editing api.py - the exact shared-file edit the host exists to forbid. How should a feature contribute its error-to-HTTP-status mapping?

state.problem: Porting 12 already-built feature branches onto the new plugin host. Survey of what each needed from the old shared api.py: 9 of 12 registered a FastAPI exception handler via @app.exception_handler for their own domain error type (RuleError, LibraryError, AccessError, CrmError, SearchError, PermissionDenied, ...). FastAPI exception handlers can only be attached to the app object, not to an APIRouter, so a feature cannot attach its own error mapping without editing api.py - the exact shared-file edit the host exists to forbid. How should a feature contribute its error-to-HTTP-status mapping?

candidate_solutions.host_exception_handlers: Extend the contract: a feature may export EXCEPTION_HANDLERS = {MyError: handler} and the host calls app.add_exception_handler for each, recording it in the registry. Small, explicit, and features keep their error vocabulary local.
candidate_solutions.raise_httpexception_in_service: Refuse the extension. Each feature converts its domain errors to fastapi.HTTPException at its own route boundary, so the app-level handler is never needed. Keeps the host smaller but pushes status codes into every route function and away from the domain module.
candidate_solutions.central_error_registry: Add a core error registry module that features edit to declare their error types, restoring a single place where all error-to-status mapping lives.

context.constraint: A feature must never edit backend/dsr/api.py or any other shared file.
context.evidence: 9 of 12 branches need it; central_error_registry is the shared-file pattern that caused the original stall.
context.stack: FastAPI; exception handlers register on app, not on APIRouter.

decision: Which approach best resolves: The host currently refuses a feature whose APIRouter prefix collides with an already mounted one. Against the real 12 branches that granularity is wrong in both directions: WF-003 (documents under rooms) and WF-005 (room CRUD) both legitimately want the /api/rooms prefix but define disjoint concrete paths, so they are wrongly refused; while WF-007 and WF-010 both want /api/library for the content library and would collide on the same concrete routes, which the prefix check happens to catch only because their prefixes matched exactly. candidate_solutions.method_and_full_path: Track the set of (method, full path) pairs across all mounted features. Two features may share a prefix if their concrete routes differ; a genuine duplicate route is reported and the later feature is skipped.
candidate_solutions.prefix_exclusivity: Keep one prefix per feature, and rename prefixes where features overlap, editing the ported features and their tests to fit. Simpler rule, forces namespace discipline.
candidate_solutions.silent_first_wins: Mount everything and rely on FastAPI's first-match-wins ordering, doing no collision detection at all.
